core: Working definition: separation of powers is the division of government into legislative, executive, and judicial branches (attributed to the Constitution's design)
The three branches, one factual line each: Congress makes the laws; the president enforces them; the courts interpret them
Why separate: liberty through divided power — Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws (1748), one line; the Federalist Papers (Federalist No. 51, 1788), one line
The U.S. design: Article I (Congress), Article II (the president), Article III (the courts) — one factual line each
Honest note: separation is never absolute — the reality check, with an original example
Honest framing: three branches, one government — no single exit
supporting: Vocabulary: branch names, vesting clause, The Spirit of the Laws, Federalist Papers
USA.gov's statement that the division exists so no individual or group holds too much power
OpenStax American Government 3e framing of the framers' concern about a too-powerful national government
outOfScope: Checks and balances (mechanisms of mutual restraint — veto, confirmation, impeachment) — sibling topic
Judicial review (Marbury v. Madison) — sibling topic
Federalism (national-state division of power) — sibling topic

claims.claim: The Constitution of the United States divides the federal government into three branches — legislative, executive, and judicial — so that no individual or group will have too much power.
The legislative branch — Congress, made up of the Senate and the House of Representatives — makes the laws; drafting proposed laws is among its key roles.
The executive branch, headed by the president, enforces and carries out the laws.
The judicial branch — the Supreme Court and the lower federal courts — interprets the meaning of laws, applies them to individual cases, and decides whether they violate the Constitution.

Montesquieu's The Spirit of the Laws (1748) is credited as the first modern formulation of the separation-of-powers doctrine: liberty is most effectively safeguarded when governmental power is separated, and the work profoundly influenced the framing of the U.S. Constitution.

Federalist No. 51 (New York Packet, February 8, 1788; commonly attributed to James Madison) defended the Constitution's division of powers, calling the separate and distinct exercise of the different powers of government essential to the preservation of liberty.
Article I of the Constitution vests all legislative powers in a Congress of the United States, consisting of a Senate and a House of Representatives.
Article II of the Constitution vests the executive power in a President of the United States.
Article III of the Constitution vests the judicial power of the United States in one Supreme Court and in such inferior courts as Congress may from time to time ordain and establish.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the branches ever act entirely apart from one another
positions: Textbook ideal: each branch has its own core function — make, enforce, interpret
Practice: functions overlap at the edges — executive agencies write rules that read like law, courts decide what statutes mean, and the president signs or rejects bills
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the division factually and adds an explicit honest note that separation is never absolute, with an original example of one law passing through all three branches. The machinery of mutual restraint is declared out of scope and pointed to the checks-and-balances sibling topic.

positions: The Library of Congress guide labels it 'Alexander Hamilton or James Madison'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson attributes the essay to the Federalist Papers generally and notes it is commonly attributed to Madison, without asserting certainty.

sourceRecords.title: Branches of the U.S. government
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A primary source, read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Confirms the Constitution divides the federal government into three branches (legislative, judicial, executive) so that no individual or group has too much power; the legislative branch is Congress (Senate and House) and drafts proposed laws; the judicial branch includes the Supreme Court and other federal courts and interprets the meaning of laws, applies laws to individual cases, and decides if laws violate the Constitution; the executive branch is the president, vice president, and cabinet, with the president heading the executive branch. Facts synthesized in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Constitution of the United States, Article I
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A primary source. Direct fetch returns 403; read via Wayback capture of the canonical URL. Supports Article I, Section 1: all legislative powers granted are vested in a Congress of the United States, consisting of a Senate and House of Representatives. Constitution text is public domain.

sourceRecords.title: Constitution of the United States, Article II
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A primary source. Direct fetch returns 403; read via Wayback capture of the canonical URL, which confirms Article II, Section 1: 'The executive Power shall be vested in a President of the United States of America.' Also cross-checked against the National Archives transcription (archives.gov/founding-docs/constitution-transcript), read live.

sourceRecords.title: Constitution of the United States, Article III
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A primary source. Direct fetch and the Wayback capture both returned 403/404 on read date; the Article III text was verified via the National Archives transcription (archives.gov/founding-docs/constitution-transcript), read live: 'The judicial Power of the United States, shall be vested in one supreme Court, and in such inferior Courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish.'

sourceRecords.title: OpenStax American Government 3e, Section 2.3 The Development of the Constitution
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A verified OER (openstax.org blocks direct fetch; read via Wayback capture of the canonical URL). Supports: the framers' chief concern was increasing national authority while ensuring the government did not become too powerful; they resolved it through a separation of powers dividing the national government into three separate branches with different responsibilities; Congress was given the power to make laws, and the executive branch (president and vice president) and the federal judiciary (notably the Supreme Court) were created respectively to enforce and interpret the laws. Facts synthesized in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Separation of powers
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B reference. Live host returns 403 to automated fetch; read via Wayback capture of the canonical URL (article last updated November 7, 2024). Supports the working definition (division of the legislative, executive, and judicial functions of government among separate and independent bodies), the attribution of the first modern formulation to Montesquieu in De l'esprit des lois (1748), his argument that liberty is most effectively safeguarded by the separation of powers, and the work's profound influence on the framing of the U.S. Constitution. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Federalist Papers: Primary Documents in American History — Federalist Nos. 51-60
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Confirms Federalist No. 51, published in the New York Packet on February 8, 1788, titled 'The Structure of the Government Must Furnish the Proper Checks and Balances Between the Different Departments,' and its argument that 'the separate and distinct exercise of the different powers of government... is admitted on all hands to be essential to the preservation of liberty.' The guide lists the author as 'Alexander Hamilton or James Madison'; the essay is commonly attributed to Madison, and the lesson notes the common attribution without asserting certainty.
